name: Thomas Gainsborough
teaser: The English portraitist who preferred painting landscapes and said so — his Blue Boy and Mrs. Graham made him the rival of Reynolds, but his heart was in the countryside. He painted with a feathery, improvisational touch that feels like drawing.

exploreAction.targetName: The Blue Boy (Huntington Library) — the fabric
exploreAction.instruction: The most famous portrait of an English child, painted to prove blue could carry a full composition. Look at the fabric: the slashed sleeves, the falling lace, the satin that seems to move. Gainsborough painted with long, feathery strokes — up close it's almost abstract.

name: Sir Joshua Reynolds
teaser: The first president of the Royal Academy and the ruler of English taste — his portraits of aristocrats, actors, and philosophers dressed them in classical robes and made them immortal. He believed in 'the grand style' and lectured about it endlessly.

exploreAction.targetName: Mrs. Siddons as the Tragic Muse (Huntington Library) — the pose
exploreAction.instruction: The great actress sits like Michelangelo's prophet Isaiah — Reynolds borrowed the pose from the Sistine Chapel and the identity from a vision of the Tragic Muse. Look at how he flatters while he immortalizes. He famously added his own signature to the hem, daring anyone to outdo it.

name: William Hogarth
teaser: The English painter who invented the moral comic strip — his series A Harlot's Progress and Marriage A-la-Mode tell stories in numbered scenes, dripping with satire, symbolism, and social criticism. He also wrote the law that made engraving copyrightable.

exploreAction.targetName: Marriage A-la-Mode series (National Gallery, London) — the details
exploreAction.instruction: Six scenes, one disastrous arranged marriage. Play detective: the dog, the gout, the nosebleed, the paintings on the walls — every object is a clue about the characters' fates. Hogarth's genius is that his 'progresses' are readable like novels, panel by panel.

name: John Everett Millais
teaser: The child prodigy who co-founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood — his Ophelia, painted with the model lying in a bathtub for months, is one of the most famous images in art. He later abandoned the brotherhood's ideals for popular success.

exploreAction.instruction: Ophelia floats mid-song, drowning, surrounded by flowers that each carry a meaning from Hamlet: pansies for thought, violets for faithfulness, a nettle for pain. Millais painted the plants from nature, species by species. The model nearly caught pneumonia lying in the cold water.

name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
teaser: The poet-painter of the Pre-Raphaelites who worshipped a single face — his muse and wife Elizabeth Siddal, and after her death, Jane Morris. His languid, red-haired women are icons of desire and grief, painted with jewel colors and heavy symbolism.

exploreAction.instruction: Painted as a memorial to Elizabeth Siddal, who died of an overdose — Rossetti cast her as Beatrice at the moment of death: a dove drops a white poppy into her hands. Look at the sundial in the background, the misty Florence behind her. Grief, made into gold and blue.

name: Edward Burne-Jones
teaser: The dreamiest of the Pre-Raphaelites — his knights, angels, and enchanted maidens inhabit a twilight world of pale skin and medieval longing. The Golden Stairs and The Beguiling of Merlin are his masterpieces; his images fed the Symbolist movement across Europe.

exploreAction.targetName: The Golden Stairs (Tate Britain) — the descent
exploreAction.instruction: A line of maidens descends a spiral staircase carrying instruments, going nowhere, meaning nothing — pure mood. Look at the repetition of their robes, their identical profile faces, the emptiness of the setting. Burne-Jones painted the feeling of a dream before you wake.

name: James Tissot
teaser: The French-English painter of Victorian high society — his pictures of fashionable women on rivers, terraces, and railway platforms are so meticulously detailed they read like photographs. Later in life he abandoned fashion for a huge illustrated Bible.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ball on Shipboard (Tate Britain) — the crowd
exploreAction.instruction: A deck party frozen mid-dance: silk dresses, champagne, rigging, and a hundred tiny social signals. Look at how Tissot documents every fabric and gesture — he was nicknamed 'the modern Hogarth.' Then notice the one figure looking straight out at you, breaking the fourth wall.

name: Frederic Leighton
teaser: The Victorian painter of marble-white nymphs and classical longing — Flaming June, his sleeping woman in orange, is one of the most reproduced paintings of the 19th century. He was the first painter ever made a lord for his art.

exploreAction.targetName: Flaming June (Museo de Arte de Ponce, Puerto Rico) — the pose
exploreAction.instruction: A sleeping woman curls into a near-impossible pose, her dress a waterfall of burning orange. Look at the plant — oleander, which means death — and the sea behind her. Leighton obsessed over the pose for months, painting it from a model who fell asleep. Sleep, beauty, mortality, all in one.

name: Lawrence Alma-Tadema
teaser: The Dutch-British painter of ancient Rome who did the archaeology himself — his marble terraces, Roman baths, and toga parties are so accurate that Hollywood later copied them. The Roses of Heliogabalus showers guests in a blizzard of petals.

exploreAction.targetName: The Roses of Heliogabalus — the petals
exploreAction.instruction: A Roman emperor suffocates his guests under tons of rose petals — Alma-Tadema had real roses shipped from the Riviera and painted petal by petal for months. Look at the marble, the water, the fruit: everything is archaeological fact except the fantasy. Then ask what the painting means.

name: John Singleton Copley
teaser: The greatest American painter before the Revolution — his portraits of Boston merchants, silversmiths, and Paul Revere are so real you can smell the workshop. He left for England and never returned, but his American portraits remain untouchable.

exploreAction.targetName: Paul Revere (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston) — the hands
exploreAction.instruction: No wig, no pose — just a working silversmith in his shirtsleeves, holding a teapot, his tools on the table. Look at the face: sharp, intelligent, watchful. Copley painted America as it actually was, and this portrait is the definitive image of the man who rode to Lexington.

name: Gilbert Stuart
teaser: The painter of the American founding fathers — his portraits of Washington, including the famous unfinished 'Athenaeum' head, became the image of the new nation (you know it from the one-dollar bill). He never finished the Washington portrait, and it made him eternal anyway.

exploreAction.targetName: The Athenaeum Portrait of George Washington (National Portrait Gallery, DC)
exploreAction.instruction: Washington sat for Stuart only three times; this head-and-shoulders was meant to be finished later and never was. Look at the skin tones, the alert eyes — a president, not a statue. Stuart made dozens of copies because buyers demanded them; the original stayed unfinished forever.

name: Thomas Eakins
teaser: The American realist who painted the body as science — his Gross Clinic shows surgeons at work in a blaze of light, his rowers and boxers move with anatomical truth. He was fired from his teaching job for demanding a male model in a female class.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gross Clinic (Philadelphia Museum of Art) — the light
exploreAction.instruction: Dr. Gross stands over an operating table, scalpel in hand, in a dark amphitheater lit by a single sky light. Look at the faces: the student who recoils, the woman who can't watch. When it was shown in 1876, Philadelphia called it too brutal to exhibit; now it's a national treasure.

name: Winslow Homer
teaser: The great American painter of the sea — he moved to a remote Maine coast and painted waves, storms, and fishermen with a brute force no one in America had attempted. The Gulf Stream shows a man adrift with sharks circling; Homer never explained it.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gulf Stream (Met, New York) — the sharks
exploreAction.instruction: A Black man lies on a broken boat, surrounded by sharks, a waterspout on the horizon. The boat has a mast with a torn sail — a reference to the Middle Passage. Look at the colors: turquoise water, white sharks, blood. Homer called it 'a matter of fact,' and refused to explain further.

name: George Bellows
teaser: The Ashcan painter of boxing and the city — his Stag at Sharkey's catches a bloody prizefight in a smoky club with a violence that thrilled America. He also painted the shocking 1913 painting of the execution of Edith Cavell.

exploreAction.targetName: Stag at Sharkey's (Cleveland Museum of Art) — the crowd
exploreAction.instruction: Two boxers tangle mid-swing while a roaring crowd presses in from all sides — you're ringside in 1909. Look at the sweat, the blood, the hats. Bellows painted the raw city with thick, fast strokes. He called the fights 'love in the raw.'

name: Charles Sheeler
teaser: The American precisionist who painted factories, grain elevators, and steamships as clean, silent cathedrals — he was also a photographer whose images of Ford's River Rouge plant blurred the line between photography and painting.

exploreAction.instruction: The River Rouge plant: clean white walls, geometric windows, a freight train — painted with a precision that makes industry look holy. Sheeler worked from his own photographs, cropping and flattening. Notice the absolute stillness: no people, no smoke, just pure American form.

name: Thomas Hart Benton
teaser: The Midwestern muralist of rolling grain and hard labor — his twisting, muscular farmers and steelworkers fill state capitol walls across America. He taught at the Kansas City Art Institute, where a young Jackson Pollock studied and chafed.

exploreAction.targetName: America Today murals (Met, New York) — the figures
exploreAction.instruction: Ten panels of 1920s America: oil rigs, cotton fields, city jazz, factory floors. Look at the bodies — bent, stretched, and coiled like springs. Benton drew from memory and from a lifetime of riding freight trains. His America is sweaty, big, and alive.

name: Charles Burchfield
teaser: The American painter who made small-town houses hum with visible energy — his watercolors show vibrating walls, singing trees, and weather as a physical force. Critics rediscovered his late, hallucinatory works as masterpieces of 20th-century mysticism.

exploreAction.targetName: The Insect Chorus or his late sun/moon paintings
exploreAction.instruction: In Burchfield's late paintings, the sun turns into a blazing disk with rays like thorns, and houses pulse with lines of force. Look at how he made a midsummer afternoon feel loud. He worked from childhood memories and a private system of symbols he never fully explained.
